original_value: Partial label learning is a weakly supervised learning framework, in which each instance is provided with multiple candidate labels while only one of them is correct. Most of the existing approaches focus on leveraging the instance relationships to disambiguate the given noisy label space, while it is still unclear whether we can exploit potentially useful information in label space to alleviate the label ambiguities. This paper gives a positive answer to this question for the first time. Specifically, if two instances do not share any common candidate labels, they cannot have the same ground-truth label. By exploiting such dissimilarity relationships from label space, we propose a novel approach that aims to maximize the latent semantic differences of the two instances whose ground-truth labels are definitely different, while training the desired model simultaneously, thereby continually enlarging the gap of label confidences between two instances of different classes. Extensive experiments on artificial and real-world partial label datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art counterparts.

result.paraphrase: Partial label learning is a weakly supervised framework in which each instance comes with multiple candidate labels, but only one is correct. Most existing methods concentrate on using relationships among instances to resolve the ambiguity in the noisy label space, yet it remains uncertain whether useful information in label space can also be exploited to reduce label ambiguity. This paper provides the first positive answer to that question. In particular, if two instances share no candidate labels, they cannot have the same ground-truth label. Leveraging these dissimilarity relations in label space, we propose a new method that maximizes the latent semantic distance between two instances whose ground-truth labels are certainly different while training the target model at the same time, thereby continuously widening the gap in label confidence between instances from different classes. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world partial label datasets show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives.
